## What is this talk about? 

* *how to* visualize findings and data
* common data types and their appropriate visualizations

## Why "plotting" does it matter?

* If no one can understand your research, then does it matter?
* Data has a story, but raw numbers can't speak and can sometimes mislead (see
Anscombe's Quartet). Visualizations bridge complex statistics and
human intuition.
* Patterns emerge in pictures, not spreadsheets. Plotting reveals hidden trends,
clusters, and outliers that a table of data will completely hide.
* A well-crafted plot builds immediate trust, credibility, and impact with your
audience.

:::notes
Plotting is not just is a fundamental part of the communication and translation
of science. Anscombe's Quartet is four datasets with identical
statistical properties (i.e., mean, variance, and correlation) but when plotted
look completely different. This dataset is standard in R and can be loaded with
the call `data(anscombe)`. Clear communication multiplies the impact of your 
research value.
:::

## What is `ggplot2`?

```{r}
#| label: generate statistics on ggplot downloads
#| echo:  FALSE
#| cache: TRUE

dl <- cran_downloads("ggplot2", when = "last-month")
totals <- aggregate(count ~ package, data = dl, FUN = sum)
ggplot_downloads <- totals$count
```


* an `R` package dedicated to visualization
* gives researchers a common grammar for constructing visualizations
* many extensions (e.g., `ggpubr`)
* base `ggplot2` has had `r format(ggplot_downloads, big.mark = ",")` downloads
in the past 30 days

:::notes
`ggplot` is one of the most downloaded packages on CRAN (don't believe me--see
the above statistic grabbed directly from CRAN's APIs).
:::

## A skeletal ggplot call `r emoji::emoji('skeleton')`

```{r demo_ggplot, eval = FALSE}
ggplot() + # call ggplot and potentially feed in data and variables to plot to specific aesthetics
  geom() + # pick a plot type. Data and variables to plot to specific aesthetics can also be assigned here
  scale() + # make adjustments to the scales
  labs() + # customize labels
  ... + # there are other options!
  theme() # add some style
```

:::notes
`ggplot()` is based on a grammar graphics -- a way of approaching describing
the construction of a graphic from common building blocks. Building a graphic
with ggplot then follows some common patterns of construction.

At its most basic, we supply ggplot with a data set and some aesthetics to map
-- that is, the variables we wish to display on the plot and how they should
appear. We then define a plot type.

Step by step this looks like:

1. call ggplot()
2. provide ggplot with a data set
3. provide ggplot with the variable(s) of interest and their aesthetic properties
4. define a plot type with geom_*plotType*()

After this, we continue to add on layers. We can add on additional `geoms`, we
can add on scale adjustments, statistical summaries etc. and finally we can
adjust how the overall presentation looks, adjusting titles, labels, legends
etc.
:::

## **NOIR**: levels of measurement

| Level        | Order | Description                 | Example          | General Note      |
| :---         | :---  | :---                        | :---             | :---              |
| **N**ominal  | N     | Classifies                  | Marital status   | Pick a category   |
| **O**rdinal  | Y     | Classifies, > < comparisons | Education        | Pick a preference |
| **I**nterval | Y     | Difference, - + comparisons | Number of people | Count something   |
| **R**atio    | Y     | Magnitude, x / comparisons  | Height           | Measure something |

:::notes
A common taxonomy (first proposed by American psychologist Stanely Smith Stevens
in his 1946 work entitled *On the Theory of Scales of Measurment* published in
the journal *Science*) breaks data into four taxonomic groups: Nominal (data
split into categories with no implicit order or hierarchy), Ordinal (categories
with a meaningful rank or order), Interval (data have ordered measurable 
intervals between values), and Ratio (interval scale with absolute zero point).

Not all visuals are appropriate for all levels. Reflecting back on our earlier
discussion of data types in R, nominal and ordinal data are generally
categorical or 'factor', interval will be classified as integers, and ratio
will be classified as double. If our data types are not properly assigned, R
will often 'coerce' the data type to something that will
work, but this isn't always successful, nor is very good practice to make the
system guess!
:::

## Read in data

```{r}
gapminder <- read.csv(file = "../../data/gapminder.csv")
gapminder_7 <- gapminder %>% filter(year == 2007) # filter to just one year
```

:::notes
By now we should be familiar enough with reading in data that we don't need to
talk about it, but I'm showing it here just in case. Today we will once again
work with the gapminder dataset.
:::

## `ggplot()`: the building block

```{r ggplot_data}
ggplot(data = gapminder)
```

:::notes
The `ggplot` call creates a 'blank slate'. It is the buildding block on which
the rest of the call rests. 

*Aside*: The core components of the `ggplot` syntax (in addition to
visualization packages in other programming languages such as Python's 
`plotnine`) are based off of a framework proposed by the scientist Hadely
Wickham (New Zealand) who is the chief scientist at Posit (the parent company
of Rstudio). The book is calle the **Grammar of Graphics**.
:::

## Adding dimensions:  `aes()` 

```{r ggplot_aes}
# aes() stands for aesthetic
ggplot(data = gapminder_7, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp))
```

:::notes
The call `aes()` links variables to visual properties (or channels) such as
shape, size, colour, or dimension. The above call sets us up with a blank grid
with `x` and `y` axis ticks corresponding to your variable values and x and y
axis labels corresponding to your variables.
:::

## Visualizing scatterplot data

```{r ggplot_point}
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point()
```

:::notes
Now we call a plot type to represent our data, in this case, a scatter plot.
:::

## The `geoms`

| `ggplot2` call                                          | type of                             |
| :---                                                    | :---                                |
| `geom_bar()`, `geom_col()`                              | bar charts                          |
| `geom_boxplot()`                                        | box-and-whisker plots               |
| `geom_histogram`, `geom_violion()`, `geom_boxplot()`    | distributions                       |
| `geom_line()`, `geom_smooth()`                          | connecting observations (trends)    |
| `geom_point()`, `geom_jitter`                           | scatter plots                       |
| `geom_map()`, `geom_sf()`                               | spatial data (rasters)              |

:::notes
There are several `geoms_` that we can choose from. They each correspond to 
different types of data we want plots. Some are good for plotting trends
(scatter plots and lines), visualizing distributions (histograms), and
understanding central tendency and spread (box-and-whisker plots).


> There are many aesthetics that we can map to `aes()` and each `geom_` will
accept different aesthetics. You can review available aesthetics using the help
pages. Those aesthetics in **bold** are required.

:::


## Categorical variables: Basic Bar Chart

```{r basic_bar}
# equivalent to the number of countries in each continent in 2007
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = continent)) +
  geom_bar()
```

:::notes
ggplot2 offers to geoms for plotting bar charts, `geom_bar()` and `geom_col()`.
Use `geom_bar()` when you don't have a count of your categories (it requires a
single categorical variable, and passes the operation off to another function
that tallies the number of observations associated with each level). And use
`geom_col()` when you have a tally per category (it requires two variables to be
passed to `aes()`, a categorical variable and a numeric variable.)

While `geom_bar()` is convenient, you'll likely want a frequency table of
corresponding values anyway, which you can the plot with `geom_col()`.
R provides an easy way to get a frequency table with the function `table()`.
:::

## Frequency table

```{r freq_table}
country_freqtable <- table(subset(gapminder, year == 2007, select = continent))

country_freqtable
```

:::notes
NA` values are dropped by default.

`ggplot()` only accepts dataframes and tibbles, so we need to convert out
table. Unless we need to preserve our dataframe, we can do this on the fly
within our call to `ggplot()`. when converting a table to a dataframe, the
variable name for the categorical variable is preserved and the count variable
is names `Freq`.
:::

```{r solution_2}
ggplot(data = as.data.frame(country_freqtable), aes(x = continent, y = Freq)) +
  geom_col()
```

## Additional aesthetics

```{r}
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point()
```

:::notes
Beyond articulating the variables on the x and y plane, we can also articulate
variables according to other aesthetic properties, such as colour,
opacity (alpha), and size.

Colour can be added with `fill` or `colour`; `fill` fills objects, such as bars
on a bar chart, colour produces a line of colour, either, for examples, around
a bar chart, or to define the colour of a line, with a point being a section of
a line.
:::

```{r}
# aes() can take the 'size' parameter which (in this case) tells ggplot
# that we want to assign the points to size 'continent' (a nominal variable)
# ...which doesn't make sense :/
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = continent)) +
  geom_point()
```

:::notes
`ggplot2` operating on a grammar of graphics, allows us to do things that are
grammatically correct, but don't necessarily make sense, such as mapping size
to a categorical variable. It will let you know, however, that something is
not quite right.

Colour, opacity, and size can be assigned either as a scale, where each value
takes on a different property, or as general property of the variable. The
former is articulated within the `aes()` call, while the latter is articulated
outside of this call, generally within the geom. The latter will override the
former if both are articulated. See, for example, the difference in the
following plots.
:::

## Playing with visual channels: `size` and `colour`

```{r}
# colour and size mapped to values
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point()

# colour mapped to continent values, size to the geom
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, colour = continent)) +
  geom_point(size = 5)

# colour and size mapped to values, but overriden by also being mapped to the geom, note also the loss of the legend
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, colour = 'pink')
```

## Much abrew about nothing: getting familiar with `RColorBrewer`

```{r, fig.height= 8}
display.brewer.all()
```

:::notes
Our scales, or how are variables are mapped, can be adjusted in many
different ways. There are scale adjustments for the variables mapped to fill,
colour, alpha, size, x, and y.

For colour, we'll use a common library `RColorBrewer`.

To view the colour palettes available from this package.
:::

## Scaling colour with `RColorBrewer`

```{r}
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point() +                           # scatterplot
  scale_size(range = c(1,15)) +            # constrain points to a common size
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") + # 'Dark2' just one available colour scheme
  scale_x_log10()                          # scale the x-axis
```

:::notes
In the following, we re-map the size range, the colour range, and apply a
log transformation to the x-axis variable to make life expectancy and
GPD per capita more comparable.
:::

## Labeling, titles, and captions

```{r}
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_size(range = c(1,15)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "GDP per Capita (2007)",
       y = "Life Expectancy",
       title = "Gapminder 2007",
       caption = "2007 life expectancy plotted against per capita GDP.",
       colour = "Continent",
       size = "Population")
```

:::notes
Labels--on the x and y axis, as well as on the other mappings (size, colour,
fill, alpha, etc.)--default to our variable names, which may not be what we
want on our graph. Titles and captions are by default blank. We can override
this with `labs()`.
:::

```{r}
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_size(range = c(1,15)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar_format(),
                breaks = breaks_width(10000)) +
  labs(x = "GDP per Capita (2007",
       y = "Life Expectancy",
       title = "Gapminder 2007",
       caption = "2007 life expectancy plotted against per capita GDP.",
       colour = "Continent",
       size = "Population")
```

## Tweaking the presentation

```{r}
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_size(range = c(1,15)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar_format(),
                breaks = breaks_width(10000)) +
  labs(x = "GDP per Capita (2007",
       y = "Life Expectancy",
       title = "Gapminder 2007",
       caption = "2007 life expectancy plotted against per capita GDP.",
       colour = "Continent",
       size = "Population") +
  theme_minimal() # this is my personal favorite
```

:::notes
x and y axis ticks and text are auto generated. The scale options allow
us to customize these, however. To do this, we need the `scales` library,
which is automatically installed with `ggplot2`. We can access scales either
by loading the library `r library(scales)` or by referencing it directly, which
has the additional benefit of prompting auto complete options. Here, we adjust
the x axis to indicate that the data should be formatted as a currency, and
update the ticks to appear every $10,000.
:::

## Themes

| `theme_` call     | look                     
| :---              | :---                     
| `theme_bw()`      | popular for publications 
| `theme_classic()` | clean, academic look     
| `theme_light()`   | subtle, professional     
| `theme_dark()`    | for dark backgrounds     

:::notes
ggplot is highly customizable. Plot themes are controlled by arguments passed
to theme. There are also several built in themes that can be used and modified.
By calling theme, you can then access any element and customize it further.
The call works by first identifying the element to customize--auto complete
will present you a series of options--then indicating what aspect of that
element you want to customize, and finally providing arguments. 
Some commonly used themes (and my personal opinion of their 'look') are shown
above.
:::

## Other `theme` options: axis orientation, legends, and grids

```{r}
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_size(range = c(1,15)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar_format(),
                breaks = breaks_width(10000)) +
  labs(x = "GDP per Capita (2007",
       y = "Life Expectancy",
       title = "Gapminder 2007",
       caption = "2007 life expectancy plotted against per capita GDP.",
       colour = "Continent",
       size = "Population") +
  theme_minimal() + # minimal theme for a clean look
  theme(
    # tilt x-axis tick labels to 45 degrees for a cleaner look
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45),
    legend.position = "left", # change position of legend
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank() # element_blank() removes visual elements
  )
```

:::notes
Sometimes when our picture (data) that we want to present gets complicated
our plots can end up getting cluttered. One common problem is that axis labels
(numbers or categories) can be quite long. `theme` gives us the option to tilt
those labels (at whatever angle we want). Additionally it gives us a way to 
position our legend and remove axis lines we don't want.
:::

## Statisical overlays & multiple geoms

```{r}
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) + # overlay with a linear model
  scale_size(range = c(1,15)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar_format(),
                breaks = breaks_width(10000)) +
  labs(x = "GDP per Capita (2007",
       y = "Life Expectancy",
       title = "Gapminder 2007",
       caption = "2007 life expectancy plotted against per capita GDP.",
       colour = "Continent",
       size = "Population") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45),
    legend.position = "left",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

:::notes
We can overlay our plot with additional geoms. Some of the geoms available
are models (for instance a linear model can be output and displayed as seen
above).
:::

## A cleaner model  

```{r}
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) + # create a lm smooth for all countries
  scale_size(range = c(1,15)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar_format(),
                breaks = breaks_width(10000)) +
  labs(x = "GDP per Capita (2007)",
       y = "Life Expectancy",
       title = "Gapminder 2007",
       caption = "2007 life expectancy plotted against per capita GDP.",
       colour = "Continent",
       size = "Population") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45),
    legend.position = "left",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```
:::notes
We can better articulate our data within the representation, by passing the
x and y variables to ggplot, but the colour and size variables to a 
specific geom. This way, only `gdpPercap` and `lifeExp` get passed to
`geom_smooth()`. In the previous example the smooth had inherited the grouping
variable (continent).
:::

## More than one plot: `facet_`

```{r}
ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_size(range = c(1,15)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar_format(),
                n.breaks = 4) +
  labs(x = "GDP per Capita (2007)",
       y = "Life Expectancy",
       title = "Gapminder 2007",
       caption = "2007 life expectancy plotted against per capita GDP.",
       colour = "Continent",
       size = "Population") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "left",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  # facet wrap creates one scatterplot (and model) per continent
  # the parameter `scales = "free_x"' tells ggplot to allow each faceted
  # plot to vary freely in the x axis (each x-axis scale is determined by the
  # spread of the data)
  facet_wrap(~ continent, scales = "free_x") 
```

:::notes
There are several ways to place more than one plot side by side. The first is
to group (facet) plots by a specific variable with either `facet_wrap()` or
`facet_grid()`.
:::

## More than one plot: `patchwork`

```{r}
le_gdp_scatter <- ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_size(range = c(1,15)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar_format(),
                n.breaks = 4) +
  labs(x = "GDP per Capita (2007",
       y = "Life Expectancy",
       title = "Gapminder 2007",
       caption = "2007 life expectancy plotted against per capita GDP.",
       colour = "Continent",
       size = "Population") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45),
    legend.position = "left",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

le_gdp_box <- ggplot(data = filter(gapminder, year == 2007), aes(x = continent, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = continent)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +   theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45),
    legend.position = "left",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

# patchwork syntax example "+" and "/"
le_gdp_scatter + le_gdp_box # side-by-side plots

le_gdp_scatter / le_gdp_box # stacked plots
```

:::notes
The second is to print several plots in a specific arrangement. There are
several tools to do this, one of which is `patchwork`.

To use patchwork, we store plots within variables, and then use basic operators
to define their relationship. Patchwork offers a lot of customization. In
general we can stack ggplot objects with patchwork either horizontally or
vertically by using the `+` or `/` operators respectively like you would
ordinary arithmetical operations.
:::
